title: A type before a person
text: Volume III opens not with a character but with a species. Hugo spends a whole Book describing 'the gamin' in general, the way a naturalist describes the sparrow, before any particular boy appears. The pause tells you the new volume is about Paris itself and the people it breeds, not only about the characters you already know.

title: A pearl in the mud
text: The gamin swears, steals a little and sings obscene songs, and yet 'has no evil in his heart'. Hugo's image is a pearl that mud cannot dissolve. It is the book's old argument in a new body: what a person is inside is not the same as the dirt society throws on him.

title: A world under the paving-stones
text: The gamin's currency of scrap copper, his insects, his imaginary monster 'the deaf thing' living in old wells: Hugo builds a whole secret economy and natural history for children nobody looks at. Notice how much of it lies underneath, in cracks, gutters and under lifted stones. The street child's Paris is the city seen from below.

title: Jokes as evidence
text: Hugo drops in two street-boy jokes, the doctor 'carrying home his own work' and 'Search me!'. He does not explain them. The jokes are his proof that the gamin has a mind as quick as Talleyrand's and is, as he says, more honest.

title: Paradise in the gallery
text: The cheap top gallery of the theatre, 'narrow, dark, fetid', is called Paradise because the children pack it with joy. It is a small instance of a pattern in the book: the lowest, darkest place turned into something radiant by the people in it.

title: The useless without the necessary
text: 'Bestow on an individual the useless and deprive him of the necessary, and you have the gamin.' He has the theatre and no bread. In one line Hugo gives you the shape of urban poverty as he sees it: not only want, but a strange mix of want and freedom.

title: Beware of the gaping gamin
text: Hugo lists Prejudice, Oppression, Tyranny and the rest, and warns them all to watch this child. The gamin is the whole of anarchy, as the idle lounger is the whole of monarchy. The street boy is presented as a political force, a witness who is quietly taking notes.

title: Jug or amphora?
text: 'The little fellow will grow up.' Hugo says chance and the spirit of Paris decide whether this lump of common clay becomes something great or something low. How much does he believe in chance here, and how much in what society chooses to do with such a child?

title: The narrator steps out
text: 'He who writes these lines has long been a prowler about the barriers of Paris.' Hugo writes in his own person about the wastelands at the city's edge, the quarries, the walls, the mills. The confession gives the description a lived-in feel, and it tells you he knows these 'limbos of Paris' at first hand.

title: The edge of the city
text: The banlieue is 'end of the grass, beginning of the pavements', neither country nor town. The reader has been here before: the Gorbeau house sat in just such a half-world. Hugo's children crowned with cornflowers belong to this in-between zone, and for them 'the universe ends there'.

title: Galley-slaves wanted
text: Under Louis XIV, Hugo says, the courts manufactured convicts to row the new galleys, and a homeless boy of fifteen could be sent to them. Under Louis XV children vanished from the streets altogether. The history lesson is pointed: the state has a long record of treating poor children as raw material.

title: All crimes begin in the child
text: 'All crimes of the man begin in the vagabondage of the child.' Hugo then makes an exception for Paris, whose air 'preserves the soul'. Hugo is asking where criminals come from, and his answer is: from neglected children. The book has already shown one child, the little Savoyard Petit-Gervais, alone on a road with a coin.

title: Hugo coins a word
text: Hugo claims the word 'gamin' first reached print in 1834 in 'Claude Gueux', which happens to be his own short story about a poor man driven to crime and execution. It is a sly bit of self-reference: he presents himself as the writer who gave this child a name.

title: Laughing at the guillotine
text: The gamin treats executions as festivals, gives the guillotine pet names and knows what every condemned man wore. Hugo does not moralise much; he lets the reader feel how strange it is that a society teaches its children to see death by law as entertainment.

title: The pear
text: From 1830 the gamin 'scrawled pears on the walls'. The pear was the famous caricature of King Louis-Philippe, whose heavy-jowled face cartoonists turned into a pear. Hugo's anecdote of the king himself helping a boy finish one shows the good-natured monarch and the mockery that surrounded him in a single scene.

title: Two things he can never get
text: The gamin longs 'to overthrow the government, and to get his trousers sewed up again'. The joke pairs revolution with mending. Both are out of reach for him, and Hugo makes the political and the domestic need sit side by side.

title: He knows every policeman
text: The gamin can name every officer in Paris and has 'special notes on each one'. Hugo has shown us a great deal of the police in this book so far, mostly from above. Here the watchers are watched, from below, by a child.

title: From Molière to Barra
text: Hugo enlists famous Parisians in the gamin's family: Molière (born Poquelin, near the market), Beaumarchais, Camille Desmoulins, and Barra, the boy drummer killed in the Revolutionary wars and made a republican martyr. The list moves from comedy to heroism, which is exactly the range he claims for the street child.

title: He amuses himself because he is unhappy
text: The Book has been funny for several chapters. Then the summing-up turns the joke inside out: 'the gamin is a being who amuses himself, because he is unhappy.' Read the earlier jokes again in that light.

title: Cured by light
text: The gamin is 'a grace to the nation, and at the same time a disease'. The cure Hugo prescribes is light, which here means schooling: 'Make men, make men.' Light in this book has meant mercy and conscience; now it also means universal education.

title: A catalogue as an argument
text: The long, dizzying list pairing ancient Rome and Greece with modern Paris is meant to overwhelm. Its point is simple: 'Seek something that Paris has not.' Paris is the whole of human history in miniature. The final sting, that Paris would miss its guillotine, brings the praise back down to earth.

title: To dare
text: 'To dare; that is the price of progress.' It is not enough for philosophers to foresee a revolution; 'it is necessary that Danton should dare it.' The chapter is a hymn to audacity, and it ends by linking Prometheus's torch with Cambronne's pipe from Waterloo.

title: A roll-call of liberty
text: Washington, Kosciusko, Bolivar, Byron at Missolonghi, John Brown at Harper's Ferry, Garibaldi: Hugo, writing in the early 1860s, ranges well beyond the novel's time. He presents Paris, with its 14th of July and its night of 4 August 1789, as the source of every later struggle for freedom.

title: Sand into crystal
text: The rabble that Cicero and Burke despised is 'vile sand' which, thrown into the furnace, becomes 'a splendid crystal' through which Galileo and Newton see the stars. Hugo keeps returning to the image of something dark becoming transparent. Here it is the poor themselves.

title: Why the whole Book
text: 'To paint the child is to paint the city.' Hugo now tells you why he spent a dozen chapters on a type: the people of Paris, even grown up, are the gamin. The sparrow was a way of studying the eagle.

title: From type to person
text: After the general portrait, one boy steps out of it, and he does not fit. He has the gamin's laugh but 'a heart absolutely sombre and empty'. Hugo built the type so that you would feel exactly how this child differs from it.

title: Orphans with a father and mother
text: 'His father did not think of him, and his mother did not love him.' The street is softer to him than his mother's heart, and yet 'his mother loved his sisters'. The book has already shown children loved and unloved under one roof. Here is another family that chooses which child to love.

title: Back to the Gorbeau house
text: The boy's visits home lead to 'that double number 50–52 with which the reader is acquainted'. Hugo returns us to the hovel where Jean Valjean and Cosette once hid, now full of strangers, with a new old portress. Places in this book are reused, and they carry their memories with them.

title: A name that breaks the thread
text: The father calls himself Jondrette and asks the portress to say he is a Pole, an Italian or a Spaniard if anyone asks. The son is called Gavroche. 'It seems to be the instinct of certain wretched families to break the thread.' Names here are not inherited but shed. Why would a man want to be anybody but himself?

title: A man out of his century
text: Marius was promised at the end of the last chapter; Hugo gives us his grandfather instead. M. Gillenormand is over ninety in 1831, with all his teeth, and he 'formerly resembled everybody, and now resembles nobody'. The detour is deliberate: before we meet the young man, we meet the world he comes out of.

title: Too poor, not too old
text: He has renounced women, he says, not because he is too old but because he is too poor. His dream is an inheritance to spend on mistresses. Hugo enjoys the old man's vitality, but notice what money means to him: not bread, as it does at the Gorbeau house, but pleasure.

title: Fleurs-de-lys sewn by convicts
text: Gillenormand's beloved boudoir is hung with straw tapestry made 'on the galleys of Louis XIV' by convicts, for a nobleman's mistress. Hugo slips it in without comment, a chapter after he told us how Louis XIV filled those galleys. The elegance of the old regime rests, quite literally, on the labour of the condemned.

title: A heap of blackguards
text: 'The French Revolution is a heap of blackguards.' Gillenormand dresses like a dandy of the Directory, owns a portrait 'of no one knows whom', and despises 1789. He is the eighteenth century surviving into the nineteenth, and his opinions are as fixed as his furniture.

title: The dancers of Voltaire's day
text: La Camargo, Mlle Sallé and La Guimard were star dancers of the Paris Opéra in the eighteenth century, celebrated by Voltaire. Gillenormand's memories are a roll-call of a vanished world of pleasure. When he sneers at Restoration ministers like Corbière and Casimir Périer as vulgar names, he is measuring the present against that lost glitter.

title: Luc-Esprit
text: His godfather named him Luc-Esprit, 'Light-Wit', expecting a genius. The chapter title holds the joke: the name is a prophecy he half fulfilled. In a book full of chosen and discarded names, here is one handed down as a hope.

title: Not seeing ninety-three twice
text: Gillenormand tells and retells how he dodged the guillotine in the Terror, and jokes that he hopes not to 'see ninety-three twice', meaning both the year 1793 and his own age. His whole political life is a reaction against one terrible year. Hugo returns to 1793 again and again in this book; here it is a private wound and a pun.

title: Comedy with an edge
text: The elixir of gold, a quack cure 'for the catastrophes of love', turns out to be perchloride of iron. Hugo plays Gillenormand's credulity for laughs, but the laughter carries a judgement: this is a mind that has stopped learning.

title: Renaming the servants
text: Every manservant is called after his province, every maid is Nicolette. The cook Olympie gets higher wages on condition she gives up her name. Gillenormand's household is a small court where the master decides who people are called. In a book where names are often lost or hidden, here they are simply confiscated.

title: A theory that became a history
text: Gillenormand's theory of marriage, let the neglected wife handle the money, 'had become his history': his second wife spent his fortune. Hugo likes this compression: a man's opinion and his fate turn out to be the same sentence.

title: Generous in his own way
text: Presented at eighty-four with a baby he cannot be the father of, Gillenormand is flattered rather than angry. When a second arrives, he pays the mother, Magnon, eighty francs a month and insists the boys be treated well. Vanity and decency are hard to pull apart in him. Hugo calls him 'kindly, abrupt, charitable'.

title: The disgrace of the family
text: One daughter married 'through love, or chance, or otherwise' a soldier of the Republic and the Empire who won the cross at Austerlitz and was made colonel at Waterloo. Her father calls him 'the disgrace of my family'. What does it tell you about Gillenormand that a hero of those wars is, for him, a shame?

title: Open only after dark
text: 'The day is vulgar,' says Gillenormand, and keeps his door shut until evening, when 'fashionable people light up their minds'. Light and darkness carry heavy meanings in this book. Here they are turned into a matter of fashion: the old world prefers candlelight to daylight.

title: Frivolous and great
text: Hugo sums him up in four words: 'frivolous and great', like his century. After five chapters of comic detail, the verdict is generous. Gillenormand is not a villain; he is a period piece with a heart.

title: Angel and goose
text: The two daughters both had wings, 'the one like an angel, the other like a goose'. The younger married her dream of a heroic figure and died; the elder never married and became 'a twilight soul'. Hugo sets two kinds of longing side by side, romantic love and social ambition, and neither ends happily.

title: He idolized him
text: Gillenormand speaks to his small grandson only with a raised cane and a list of insults. Then comes the turn: 'He idolized him.' Love in this house speaks in the wrong voice. Compare the Jondrette home a few chapters back, where there are no insults and no love at all.

title: Old man and spinster
text: Hugo points out the parallel himself: Gillenormand keeps his daughter beside him as Monseigneur Bienvenu kept his sister. 'Two weaknesses leaning on each other.' The echo invites comparison between the two households, the saint's and the worldly old man's.

title: An ultra-royalist salon
text: Madame de T.'s salon is a nest of 'ultras', royalists more royal than the king, who think Louis XVIII a Jacobin and pin their hopes on his brother, the future Charles X. They sing a version of the revolutionary song 'Ça ira' with the Bonapartists hanging from lamp-posts in place of the aristocrats. 'Songs are like the guillotine.'

title: A thief is admitted, provided he be a god
text: The Comte de Lamothe, connected with the scandal of Marie-Antoinette's diamond necklace, is honoured in this salon because his name is Valois. High society, Hugo says, admits a thief if he has the right name. Set that beside the yellow passport that shut every door on a convict.

title: Poor child
text: The handsome boy of seven hears the ladies murmur 'What a pity! Poor child!' because his father is 'a brigand of the Loire', one of Napoleon's officers. What does it do to a child to be pitied, in his own hearing, for who his father is?

title: The gardener, then the soldier
text: Hugo shows us a shy old man growing tulips at Vernon, gentle enough that 'a child could make him give way'. Only then does he unroll the campaigns: Lodi, Austerlitz, Eylau, Moscow, Waterloo. The order matters. We meet the goodness before the glory, so the 'brigand of the Loire' is a gardener before he is a legend.

title: Hugo's uncle in the cemetery
text: At Eylau, Pontmercy is 'in the cemetery where ... Captain Louis Hugo, the uncle of the author of this book' held out with eighty-three men. Hugo's father was himself a Napoleonic general. The aside tells you this chapter is family history as well as fiction: the Bonapartist father is a figure Hugo knew from the inside.

title: Am I permitted to wear my scar?
text: The Restoration refuses to recognise the rank and title Napoleon gave him at Waterloo, and threatens to prosecute him for wearing his rosette. He sends back letters addressed to 'Commandant'. The quarrel is over a name and a title, and the colonel's question to the Crown Attorney turns it into a question about his body: can the state disown his wounds too?

title: Behind a pillar at Saint-Sulpice
text: The colonel gave up his son so the boy would inherit, and now slips into Paris every few months 'like a criminal breaking his ban' just to watch him at mass. The scarred veteran is 'afraid of that old spinster'. The book has shown a parent sacrificing everything for a child before, and the picture of the hidden, watching father is close to unbearable.

title: Letters read and unread
text: Twice a year Marius sends dictated letters; his father answers 'with very tender letters which the grandfather thrust into his pocket unread'. Hugo makes the whole tragedy of the family visible in one gesture. Words of love exist, and they are stopped in a pocket.

title: Waterloo, from the other side
text: Hugo now confirms what the Waterloo chapters showed us: the officer pulled from the sunken road of Ohain was Georges Pontmercy, and he is Marius's father. The reader saw what happened in that ravine at night, and who was there. Marius has never been told any of it.

title: Phantoms round a dying fire
text: To the small boy, the old ladies of the salon, with Biblical-sounding names and gowns of no colour, are 'phantoms', and the room lets in 'more night than day'. Hugo calls it 'a mummified society'. The child who arrived 'all joy and light' becomes grave in this dimness.

title: What 'ultra' meant
text: Hugo explains the word: to be ultra is to find the Pope not papist enough and the King not royal enough, 'to be so strongly for, as to be against'. The ultras dominated the early Restoration (1814–1820). Then came the 'doctrinarians', moderate royalists who argued for accepting all of French history, fleurs-de-lys and Napoleonic N's alike.

title: Affection for what he mocks
text: Hugo says he writes of this world 'without any bitter or derisive idea', because it touches his mother, who was a royalist. It is a rare personal admission. He can satirise the salon and still insist it 'had a grandeur of its own'.

title: Cold and ardent
text: Marius grows up a fanatical royalist, unloving to his grandfather and 'gloomy' about his father. Hugo's portrait is a list of contradictions: 'cold and ardent, noble, generous, proud'. Notice that his opinions are the air he was given to breathe. Hugo is showing how a young man's politics are made for him.

title: He no longer expects you
text: Marius takes the slow coach. Hugo notes that a night diligence would have brought him in time, and that 'neither Marius nor M. Gillenormand thought of making inquiries'. The colonel dies running to meet a son who is still on the road. The tear on the dead man's cheek 'was his son's delay'.

title: A dropped hat
text: Marius, ashamed of feeling so little, drops his hat to look overcome. Hugo does not condemn him outright: 'was it his fault?' The small, false gesture is more painful than any show of grief would be, because it is true to a boy who was taught not to love this man.

title: The note
text: The colonel's last words to his son are a title and a debt. Marius is to bear the barony, and to do Thénardier 'all the good he can' for saving his father's life at Waterloo. The reader remembers what Thénardier was actually doing on that battlefield. Marius keeps the paper out of 'vague respect for death'.

title: The garden goes to nettles
text: After the burial the sword and uniform are sold to an old-clothes dealer, the neighbours pillage the rare flowers, and the rest 'turned to nettles and weeds'. The colonel's two lives, the soldier's and the gardener's, are scattered within days. 'In three forgotten.'

title: The same pillar
text: Marius kneels 'behind a pillar' in the very chapel where his father used to hide to watch him. Hugo lets the place do the work: the son stands, without knowing it, where the father stood. A chair with a name on it sets the whole revelation going.

title: A father who loved you dearly
text: In a few sentences a stranger gives Marius what his family withheld for ten years: proof that his father adored him. 'A man is not a monster because he was at Waterloo.' The old warden is no political thinker, and that is the point: plain decency sees through what opinion has hidden.

title: Some love affair
text: Marius invents a hunting party and Gillenormand winks: 'Some love affair!' The old man reads every absence as gallantry. Hugo will milk this misreading, and the comedy is sharpened by our knowing that the passion is for a dead father.

title: Conversion by reading
text: Marius changes his politics in a library, reading the Moniteur, memoirs and bulletins until his father's name gives him a week's fever. Hugo traces the stages carefully because, he says, it is 'the history of many minds of our day'. A young royalist becomes a Bonapartist and a republican by meeting history in documents.

title: Stars and a sun
text: Where Marius expected 'a guillotine in the twilight' and 'a sword in the night', he sees stars, Mirabeau, Danton, Robespierre, and a sun, Napoleon. The scene of conversion is a night window with Jupiter blazing. Hugo writes the change as a passage from darkness into dazzling light, and warns that dazzlement is not yet clear sight.

title: He went too far
text: Hugo openly criticises his hero: like 'all new converts', Marius admits 'force' alongside 'genius' and 'neglected the attenuating circumstances'. The narrator lets us share Marius's thrill and keeps a cooler head himself. 'Progress is not accomplished in one stage.'

title: A hundred visiting cards
text: Marius orders a hundred cards reading 'Le Baron Marius Pontmercy', and then, knowing nobody, keeps them in his pocket. The title his father bled for becomes the visible sign of the son's new self. It is touching and a little absurd, as Hugo means it to be.

title: The search at Montfermeil
text: Obeying the note, Marius goes to Montfermeil to find Thénardier and finds the inn closed and its keeper vanished. The reader knows more than Marius about that inn and about that 'sergeant'. Hugo leaves the irony unspoken.

title: A comic spy
text: Aunt Gillenormand sends the lancer Théodule to follow Marius and find his 'lass'. Argus snores all night. Hugo builds a light farce out of the family's assumption that a young man's secret must be a woman, and the farce is there to make the last line land.

title: The lass was a grave
text: Marius buys the finest flowers from a peasant girl, skirts the church and kneels on a grave marked 'Colonel Baron Pontmercy'. The chapter's last sentence turns everything the family assumed upside down. The love Marius has been hiding is for a father he met only as a corpse.

title: Names chosen and endured
text: 'Marius! what an ugly name!' says the aunt; 'I would rather be called Alfred,' says Théodule. A trivial exchange, in a chapter where the name on a cross is what matters most. Names in this family are a field of battle, and the dead colonel has won this one.

title: The portrait that was a testament
text: Gillenormand seizes the black shagreen case expecting a mistress's portrait and finds the colonel's note: 'my son shall take it and bear it.' The old man and his daughter sit with their backs to each other for an hour. The dead man has spoken in their own house.

title: I am your father
text: 'It means that I am the son of my father.' 'I am your father.' The whole quarrel of the generations is in these two lines. Two men who love the same boy claim him, and the boy has to choose between 'a sacred grave' and 'hoary locks'.

title: A man four years dead
text: Marius, unable to insult his grandfather or leave his father unavenged, shouts 'Down with the Bourbons, and that great hog of a Louis XVIII!' Hugo deflates it at once: Louis XVIII 'had been dead for four years; but it was all the same to him.' The outburst is political in form and purely personal in content.

title: What happened to the paper?
text: Nicolette drops the medallion on the dark stairs and it is never found. Marius is sure Gillenormand burned 'his father's testament'. Hugo tells us it was probably an accident. What does it say about Marius that he assumes the worst, and about how quarrels grow on 'petty fatalities'?

title: Secret societies of the Restoration
text: Hugo mentions the German Tugendbund and the Italian Carbonari, real secret societies that plotted against the post-Napoleonic order. The Friends of the A.B.C. are his invention, but they are modelled on the student and worker clubs of 1820s and 1830s Paris. The pun is the key: 'A.B.C.' sounds like 'abaissé', the abased, meaning the people.

title: A group portrait
text: Hugo introduces nine young men one after another, each with a role: Enjolras the logic of the Revolution, Combeferre its philosophy, Courfeyrac the centre, Feuilly the outside world, Grantaire the doubter. It reads like a painted group portrait. Each figure is defined by what he believes and how he believes it.

title: Conflagration or dawn
text: Enjolras would follow Saint-Just; Combeferre prefers Condorcet. Combeferre asks why light must come from a fire: 'A conflagration can create an aurora, no doubt, but why not await the dawn?' The two friends hold the book's old question about progress: whether it must come through violence or can come through education.

title: Names worn and shed
text: Courfeyrac drops his 'de' because the liberals of his day thought the particle unfashionable. Lesgle's family name came from 'Lesgueules' and became 'l'Aigle', the eagle; his friends call him Bossuet because he is 'de Meaux', like the great preacher. Grantaire signs himself with a rebus: R (in French, 'grand R' sounds like Grantaire). These students play with names as freely as Hugo does.

title: The doubter and the believer
text: Grantaire believes in nothing except his glass and Enjolras. 'No one loves the light like the blind man.' Enjolras scorns him, and Grantaire still says 'What fine marble!' Hugo makes their friendship a study in opposites: faith without warmth on one side, warmth without faith on the other.

title: Poland, 1772
text: Feuilly, the self-taught orphan fan-maker, rages over the partition of Poland among Russia, Prussia and Austria in 1772, which he calls the model of every later crime against nations. Poland's cause was a passion of French liberals throughout the 1830s. The orphan who 'adopted the peoples' turns a private loss into a political love.

title: A name answers for a name
text: Bossuet answers 'Present!' for Marius at roll call, is caught when his own name, Laigle, is called, and gets struck off. 'If you are Pontmercy, you are not Laigle.' Hugo's comic set-piece turns on the same thing as the darker plots of the book: one man answering to another man's name.

title: Chance as a host
text: Marius has left his grandfather's with thirty francs and no idea where to go; a name sewn on his bag and a lounger in a café doorway give him a home and friends by evening. Hugo often lets chance shape lives. Here it is kindly, and it brings Marius to the very group the previous chapter described.

title: Jean-Jacques and his children
text: Walking down the Rue Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Courfeyrac jokes that Rousseau sent his own babies to the foundling hospital. Enjolras rebukes him: 'He denied his own children, that may be; but he adopted the people.' In a book full of abandoned and adopted children, the remark lands with weight. Is it a defence or an accusation?

title: Bonaparte, not the Emperor
text: Marius has just become a 'democrat-Bonapartist', which Courfeyrac calls 'the gray hue of a reassured rat'. Among these republicans nobody says 'the Emperor', and Enjolras says 'Buonaparte' like a royalist. Marius thought his conversion had settled him. Now the ground shifts again.

title: A room full of conversations
text: Hugo moves round the back room corner by corner: Grantaire's drunken tirade, a vaudeville being plotted, a duel discussed, dominoes and love, pagan gods, and finally politics. The effect is of standing in a noisy café and catching fragments. Serious and silly talk share the same tables, as they do among the young.

title: Grantaire's despair
text: Under the jokes, Grantaire's speech is a sweeping 'All is vanity': every virtue borders a vice, history repeats itself, victory is stupid, 'man is a failure'. It is the most bleakly sceptical voice we have heard in the book. Hugo puts it in the mouth of a drunk, but he gives it real wit and real learning.

title: Burning the Charter
text: The Charter of 1814 was the constitution Louis XVIII 'granted' to France. Its Article 14 let the king rule by decree in emergencies, and in 1830 Charles X used it to suspend liberties, which set off the July Revolution. Courfeyrac's point is that a constitution handed down by a king can be taken back by him: 'By the side of the hand which gives there is the claw which snatches back.'

title: To be free
text: Marius's long, dazzling hymn to Napoleon, codes, bulletins, Austerlitz, 'the archangel of war', ends with 'what greater thing is there?' Combeferre answers in three words: 'To be free.' Hugo lets the cold, simple reply cut through the epic. Glory and liberty are not the same thing.

title: My mother is the Republic
text: Combeferre goes down the stairs singing a song about choosing one's mother over Caesar's glory. Marius, who never knew his mother, repeats 'My mother?' Then Enjolras: 'Citizen, my mother is the Republic.' The book keeps mixing family love with political love. Here a cause is offered in place of a parent.

title: Napoleon's numbers
text: Courfeyrac plays with 18: the 18th Brumaire (Napoleon's coup in 1799), the 18th of June (Waterloo), Louis XVIII. Enjolras turns the game into a verdict: 'the crime and the expiation'. The word 'crime' is what brings Marius to his feet.

title: Doubly isolated
text: Too daring for his grandfather, too old-fashioned for his friends, Marius stands 'between two religions'. Hugo compares him to earth torn open by the plough: he feels only the wound for now. He also fears that moving forward may take him further from his father, whose cause he has only just embraced.

title: Never
text: Courfeyrac offers a loan: 'Never.' The aunt sends six hundred francs in gold and Marius sends it back with three francs to his name. Pride is his whole fortune. The scene is funny (he forgets the hotel bill) and also a little alarming. Hugo lets you admire the refusal and doubt its wisdom.

title: The crucible
text: Poverty is 'a crucible into which destiny casts a man, whenever it desires a scoundrel or a demigod'. Hugo has shown poverty breaking people in this book. Now he shows it forging one, and insists on the 'obscure heroes' of daily privation who never get a trumpet blast.

title: Clothed with the night
text: Courfeyrac's old coat, turned, comes out green, so Marius goes out only after dark, when it looks black. 'As he wished always to appear in mourning, he clothed himself with the night.' One small, exact detail holds grief for his father, poverty and pride together.

title: A cutlet for three days
text: Meat on the first day, fat on the second, bone on the third. Hugo makes poverty concrete with a menu. The young man bowing to the butcher's wife with his books under his arm is comic and dignified at once.

title: A baron and a lawyer
text: Gillenormand tears up Marius's letter and is overheard talking to himself: 'one cannot be a baron and a lawyer at the same time.' He is still thinking about his grandson, and still in his own terms. Is he angry, or hurt, or both?

title: Poverty as a budget
text: Breakfast four sous, dinner sixteen, rent thirty francs, three shirts in rotation: Hugo does the sums. Seven hundred francs a year, six hundred and fifty spent, and 'he was rich'. The accounting makes Marius's dignity measurable. It also shows how thin the line is between getting by and going under.

title: Back at the Gorbeau house
text: Marius's 'den minus a fireplace' is in the Gorbeau house, the same hovel where the Jondrettes live at the end of the corridor. Hugo told us so in passing when Gavroche went home to visit. Now we see the young man settled there. The building keeps gathering lives.

title: A creditor is worse than a master
text: Marius never owes a sou. 'A debt was, to him, the beginning of slavery': a master owns your body, a creditor your dignity. His pride is a kind of armour against what poverty does to the soul, and Hugo admires it while noting its stiffness: he was 'timid even to rudeness'.

title: The lesser altar
text: Marius keeps a shrine in his heart with two altars, the great one for his father and a smaller one for Thénardier, the sergeant he believes carried the colonel out of the grapeshot. He spends three years and his savings searching for him. The reader has seen what Thénardier did that night at Waterloo. The gap between what Marius reveres and what we know is painful to watch.

title: No grandfather who does not adore
text: Hugo now shows us what Marius cannot see. Gillenormand idolizes him, misses him, asks himself whether he would turn him out again, and his 'aged head ... replied sadly no'. His grief is like a furnace 'which consumes its own smoke'. Two proud men are each waiting for the other to move.

title: Work which makes him free
text: Poverty in youth, Hugo says, strips life bare and drives the soul toward the ideal. The poor young man thanks God for 'work, which makes him free; and thought, which makes him dignified'. It is one of Hugo's great set-pieces, and it is also a portrait of Hugo's own romantic ideal of the poor student.

title: A gentle criticism
text: Hugo does not let Marius off. Contemplation 'ends by becoming one of the forms of idleness'; Marius stopped too soon, refused a good post to keep his liberty, and spends whole days in reverie. The narrator likes his hero and still marks his weakness.

title: The candle, not the someone
text: Mabeuf 'operated on me for a cataract', says Marius. Hugo corrects him: the old warden enlightened him 'as does a candle which someone brings; he had been the candle and not the someone'. Light in this book often comes through people who do not know they carry it.

title: A bouquinist
text: Mabeuf is neither royalist nor Bonapartist nor anarchist; he is a 'bouquinist', a lover of old books. He cannot see why men hate each other over charters when there are mosses to look at. After chapters of fierce opinions, Hugo gives us a man with none, and treats him tenderly.

title: The slow slide
text: His brother dies, a notary fails, the July Revolution kills the market for his Flora, and Mabeuf moves from house to cheaper house, selling his prints and furniture. Hugo describes poverty arriving gradually in a man too absorbed to notice: 'we are the stake, and we look on at the game with indifference'.

title: Indigo and the dragon
text: Mabeuf's dream is to grow indigo in France; on moving day he cheers his servant with 'We have the indigo!' Then he mishears 'dragoon' as 'dragon' and drifts into the legend of Buddha converting a fire-breathing dragon. His innocent pleasures are made of plants and books, and of the hope that monsters can be tamed by gentleness.

title: A house called Austerlitz
text: Mabeuf ends up in a cottage in the village of Austerlitz near the Salpêtrière, 'a brawling name which was ... extremely disagreeable to him'. The district was named after Napoleon's victory. Hugo enjoys the joke: the man who hates guns lives under the name of the Emperor's greatest battle.

title: Your conscience? No, your boots
text: Marius visits his father's old generals only on freezing nights, so that his boots will shine. 'In a drawing-room you may be soiled everywhere except on your shoes.' A light remark, but it states a truth the book has been driving at: society judges the surface.

title: The party of humanity
text: After 1830 Marius has 'no longer any opinions, he had sympathies'. Out of humanity he chooses France, out of France the people, out of the people the woman. His politics have become a kind of pity. Hugo also says a person is best judged by what he dreams, since 'our chimaeras are the things which the most resemble us'.

title: Do not tell them it was I
text: Hearing that the Jondrettes are being evicted for twenty francs, Marius, who has thirty, pays their rent and gives them five francs more, on condition they are not told who paid. He hardly knew he had neighbours. Secret charity has been the mark of goodness in this book from its first pages.

title: For Marius, read Théodule
text: The aunt's plan is to replace one young man with another, like correcting a misprint. The scheme fails in the most comic way: Gillenormand forgets the lancer is in the room and rants at the absent Marius instead. Théodule agrees with every word, and gets called a fool for it.

title: Students deliberate
text: The newspaper reports students meeting at the Panthéon about the National Guard's cannon in the Louvre courtyard. After July 1830 the citizen militia and the new government quarrelled over arms, and student gatherings were constant. Gillenormand's tirade lumps them with Hernani, Hugo's own scandalous 1830 play: 'Antitheses! Abominations which are not even written in French!'

title: Ranting at an empty chair
text: Every insult Gillenormand throws is aimed at Marius: 'Ah! Marius! Ah! you blackguard!' He cannot stop thinking of him. The comedy is real, but so is the grief underneath it. The yes-man Théodule is useless precisely because he is no substitute for the boy who argued back.

title: A misunderstanding with every girl
text: Marius thinks girls turn to laugh at his clothes; in fact they turn to look at him. Hugo makes his shyness a comedy of misreading. Courfeyrac calls him 'Monsieur l'Abbé'. The young man who can read a whole history of the Empire cannot read a glance.

title: Mademoiselle Lanoire and Monsieur Leblanc
text: Courfeyrac nicknames the pair on the bench from their clothes and hair: Miss Black for the girl's merino gown, Mr White for the man's white hair. 'This nickname became a law in the default of any other name.' Hugo adopts it too. In a book full of aliases, here is one invented by a joker and accepted by everyone, including the narrator.

title: A tidy widower
text: Marius sees a man of about sixty with the air of a retired soldier, dressed with odd care, who never meets anyone's eye and looks at the girl with 'ineffable paternity'. Hugo tells us almost nothing else. What do you make of a man who seems to want so badly not to be noticed?

title: Her April had arrived
text: In six months the thin, awkward girl has become beautiful. Hugo compares it to three days of April covering a tree with blossom, and to a poor man suddenly coming into an income. Notice he describes her almost entirely through Marius's eyes, feature by feature, the way a young man would look.

title: Not yet
text: She looks at him 'indifferently', as she would look at a marble vase, and he 'thought about something else'. Hugo builds the beauty up and then refuses the spark. The delay is deliberate: he is about to show us love starting, and he wants us to see the moment before.

title: A glance like dawn
text: The two glances meet, and the girl's eye is no longer a child's but 'a mysterious gulf which had half opened'. Hugo calls that first look 'like the dawn in the sky'. Then he adds that love is 'that sombre flower, impregnated with perfume and with poison'. Light and shadow arrive together.

title: From glance to wardrobe
text: The chapter's climax is a glance; its last paragraph is Marius inspecting his worn knees and pale elbows. Hugo cuts from the sublime to the ridiculous on purpose. The first sign of love in a poor young man is shame about his clothes.

title: Hannibal marched on Rome
text: Marius 'marched on the bench' in his new coat like Hannibal on Rome, and retreated before reaching it. Hugo writes the whole approach as a military campaign, with hesitations, advances and a dash 'under the cannon of the place'. The mock-heroic tone lets us laugh at the lover and still feel his terror.

title: Irreverence in a nickname
text: For the first time, Marius feels it is rude to call the gentleman 'M. Leblanc', even in his head. A name invented as a student joke now seems disrespectful because the man has become someone who matters to him. Hugo keeps showing how names change weight with feeling.

title: A vague blue light
text: The girl seems to fill the end of the alley 'with a vague blue light'; soon it is 'that bench which was surrounded by an aureole'. Marius does not look at her directly. He sees a radiance. Love in Hugo is described in the vocabulary of light.

title: Ma'am Bougon gives chase
text: The portress is staggered that Marius wears his best coat three days running and tries to follow him, 'a hippopotamus undertaking the pursuit of a chamois'. Hugo uses the outside world's view to measure how strange Marius has become. Courfeyrac even renames her: her real name is Burgon.

title: Melancholy eyes, merry smile
text: Hugo's only criticism of her beauty is that her gaze is melancholy while her smile is merry, which gives her face 'a rather wild effect'. What might make a young girl's eyes sad while her mouth laughs?

title: A glance is a spark
text: 'When the mine is charged, when the conflagration is ready, nothing is more simple. A glance is a spark.' Hugo compares a woman's glance to gears that seize you and carry you 'from torture to torture', ending either 'disfigured with shame, or transfigured by passion'. He takes love as seriously as revolution, and uses the same images of mines and fire.

title: The symptoms of love
text: Marius treats Courfeyrac to dinner, tips six sous, praises a political speech, laughs uproariously, embraces a stranger from the provinces, and announces that 'it is very agreeable, all the same to have the cross!' His friends notice. 'That's queer!' 'No, that's serious.' Hugo shows the inner state through behaviour that makes no sense to anyone else.

title: Dust on his boots
text: In the middle of his ecstasy, Marius is 'horribly vexed because there was dust on his boots', and sure she noticed. The boots have been a measure of dignity since the generals' parties. Now they are a measure of love.

title: Something was required in the foreground
text: Hugo explains that Marius's worship of his father had retreated into the depths of his soul, like all religions, and left the foreground empty. 'Love came.' The young man who lived for a dead father now lives for a living girl. Hugo presents it as a natural succession.

title: U. F.
text: Marius finds a white handkerchief marked U. F. and decides she is called Ursule. He sleeps with it under his lips. Hugo then tells us flatly that it 'belonged to the old gentleman'. The lover's whole edifice stands on a misreading. Names, once again, are guessed rather than known.

title: Three blunders
text: Hugo counts Marius's mistakes like a strategist: falling for the 'ambush' of the bench by the Gladiator, leaving when the father came alone, and soon a third. M. Leblanc changes benches and stops bringing his daughter. Something is being tested, and Marius does not see it.

title: Jealous of the wind
text: A gust lifts her dress and Marius is furious with her, although 'there had been but one culprit, the wind'. Then he wants to exterminate an old one-armed, wooden-legged veteran who winks at him. Hugo is laughing at his hero, and at the 'Bartholo who exists in Cherubin', the jealous old guardian inside the young lover.

title: Their first quarrel
text: The 'quarrel' is one sullen look from Marius and one raised eyebrow from her. They have never spoken. How much of this love affair is happening between two people, and how much inside Marius's head?

title: Are you a police spy?
text: Marius follows them home and questions the porter, who asks if he is a police spy. Seen from outside, the lover's devotion looks exactly like surveillance. The man on the third floor is 'a very kind man who does good to the unfortunate, though not rich himself'.

title: A window without a light
text: For a week Marius stands under the window watching the red lamp and the passing shadows. Then one night there is no light, and the next day the porter says they have moved, leaving no address. Hugo ends Book VI on a dark window. Someone has taken pains to disappear.

title: Why move?
text: M. Leblanc stared at Marius at the gate; the next day they stopped coming, and within a week they were gone. What would make a quiet, kindly man of modest means flee his home because a young man followed his daughter?

title: A new Book, a new depth
text: Book VII opens with a digression. Hugo takes a theatre term, the 'third lower floor' beneath the stage, and applies it to society. Above are the 'mines' of religion, philosophy and revolution, where people dig for the future. The digression sets the scale for what comes next: we are going down.

title: The starry eye and the shadowy eye
text: All the diggers of the upper mines, from Huss and Luther down to Marat and Babeuf, share one trait: disinterestedness. 'Venerate the man ... who has this sign—the starry eye.' Below them lies a mine where light goes out. Hugo divides people by what their eyes seek, the infinite or nothing at all.

title: Darkness that holds light
text: 'In the sacred shadows there lies latent light.' The catacombs where the first Christians prayed were 'the vaults of the world'. Not every darkness in this book is evil. Some of it is where light is being prepared.

title: The only social peril is darkness
text: In the lowest mine, each one is for himself, and the 'I' 'howls, seeks, fumbles, and gnaws'. Its two stepmothers are ignorance and misery. Hugo's cure is the one he named for the gamin: 'Destroy the cavern Ignorance and you destroy the lair Crime.' The argument of the whole novel is compressed into these pages.

title: The same clay
text: 'Humanity is identity. All men are made of the same clay.' Hugo refuses the idea of born criminals. What turns a man evil is the blackness of ignorance working into him. The book has already shown a man hardened in prison and then turned by a single act of mercy.

title: Lacenaire
text: 'From that vault Lacenaire emerges.' Pierre-François Lacenaire was a real murderer, guillotined in 1836, who became a celebrity by posing as a poet and a philosopher of crime. Hugo mentioned him as a gamin earlier. He stands for the criminal who is all appetite and no ideal.

title: Four portraits of the underworld
text: Gueulemer is all muscle, Babet all talk, Claquesous all darkness, Montparnasse all vanity. Hugo paints each as a type, as he did with the gamin and the students. The four together make a counter-portrait to the Friends of the A.B.C.: another group of young and not-so-young men, organised for the opposite end.

title: A Cain from an Abel
text: Montparnasse, not yet twenty, handsome, with spring in his eyes, became a murderer through the wish to be well dressed: 'the height of elegance is idleness; idleness in a poor man means crime.' Compare Marius, also poor and handsome, who chose hunger over debt. Hugo sets two young men on either side of the same choice.

title: Claquesous is night
text: He appears only after dark, speaks with his back turned, puts on a mask if a candle comes near, and throws his voice like a ventriloquist. Nobody knows if he has a name, a voice or a face. He is the darkness of Book VII given human form, a man made entirely of hiding.

title: Lost like a handkerchief
text: Babet 'had been married and had had children. He did not know what had become of his wife and children. He had lost them as one loses his handkerchief.' The joke is savage. It joins a list of fathers in this book who do not think of their children.

title: Patron-Minette
text: The gang's name is old slang for the early morning, the hour when night creatures part. Vidocq, mentioned here, was the real ex-convict who became head of the Paris detective police. Hugo blends fact and fiction: Lacenaire's 'Perhaps it was Patron-Minette' gives his invented gang a place in the true crime record of the 1830s.

title: A roll-call of aliases
text: Printanier, Bigrenaille, Mardisoir, Les-pieds-en-l'Air, and Boulatruelle, 'the road-mender already introduced' at Montfermeil. 'These names have faces attached. They do not express merely beings, but species.' The underworld is a place where names are worn, swapped and lent like disguises.

title: Light up society from below
text: Kill the individuals and 'the tribe subsists'; these men are born again from 'the social ooze' as long as society stays as it is. Hugo's remedy is not the police but light: 'Not a single bat can resist the dawn.' He is arguing that crime is a social product, which a social cure can end.

title: A lost dog
text: With the girl gone, Marius is no longer the bold defier of fate but 'a lost dog'. Nature, once full of lights and voices, 'now lay empty'. To every thought he answers 'What is the use?' Hugo shows how love has taken over the place where his ideas and plans used to be.

title: A white-haired workman
text: Marius glimpses a man in workman's clothes and cap, with very white hair and M. Leblanc's profile, walking as if in painful thought. 'What signified that disguise?' He decides it was only a resemblance. Was it?

title: Where lost women are found
text: At the ball at Sceaux, Grantaire mutters that this is 'where all lost women are found'. The pun is cruel and exact: Marius is looking for a lost girl among the 'lost' women of popular Paris. He walks home alone through the night, as he did after the Café Musain.

title: Candlemas
text: It is the 2nd of February, Candlemas, the feast of light, whose 'treacherous sun' promises six more weeks of cold. Hugo quotes the old almanac rhyme about the bear going back into its cave. Marius, emerging from his own 'cave' into the dusk, is about to have his darkness interrupted.

title: Angels and ghouls
text: Two ragged girls fleeing the police jostle Marius and drop a packet. Then he passes a child's coffin lit by a candle and thinks: 'There is one thing sadder than to see one's children die; it is to see them leading an evil life.' His last thought sets the Luxembourg girl against these: 'formerly they were angels and now they are ghouls'. Is that fair to them?

title: Four letters, one hand
text: Don Alvarès the Spanish royalist, Mistress Balizard the abandoned mother of six, Genflot the playwright, Fabantou the actor: four begging letters tuned to four kinds of donor, each claiming the cause the reader is likely to pity. Hugo reproduces the spelling mistakes with relish. Then Marius notices the same paper, the same tobacco smell, the same errors.

title: Charity as a market
text: The letters show a man who studies the rich the way a salesman studies customers: legitimism for the marquise, motherhood for the countess, flattery for the merchant who fancies himself a patron of letters, philosophy for the churchgoer. Poverty here has become a trade in identities. 'P.S. Even if it is only forty sous.'

title: Fifty years mingled with fifteen
text: The elder Jondrette girl stands in the doorway in a chemise and petticoat, with the body of a girl and 'the look of a corrupt old woman'. Hugo insists that she 'had not come into the world to be homely'. Poverty has aged her, and the traces of what she might have been make it worse.

title: A father who uses his daughters as the stake
text: Jondrette sends his girls with the letters 'at their risk and peril'; 'he was playing a game with fate, and he used them as the stake'. Marius sees 'impure and innocent monsters produced by misery'. The book has shown a mother sell everything for a child. Here a father spends his children.

title: I know how to read, I do!
text: The girl reads a line about Hougomont, writes 'The bobbies are here' with no spelling mistakes, and says 'We have not always been as we are now. We were not made—' before she breaks off with 'Bah!' Hugo lets her pride in her schooling stand as a sign of a better past she cannot finish describing.

title: You are a very handsome fellow
text: She knows his name, follows his walks to Mabeuf's, and likes his tumbled hair. Marius steps back and answers with 'cool gravity'. He is so absorbed in a girl he has never spoken to that he hardly sees the one who has just told him she watches him.

title: The sun is shining
text: Marius gives her five of his last francs and keeps sixteen sous for his dinner. 'Good! the sun is shining!' she cries. Then she seizes a mouldy crust: 'it breaks my teeth!' Her account of nights under the bridges, stars like smoking lamps and the river that looks too cold to drown in, is one of the most frightening descriptions of hunger in the book.
